To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) NK cell responses against allogeneic cells, but not autologous cells, are important to protect against HIV-1 infection and to slow HIV-1 disease progress; 2) the NK cell responses are mediated by activating KIRs in the presence of HLA class I ligands; 3) these NK cell responses are important in both HIV-1 transmission and HIV-1 disease; 4) these NK cell mechanisms are important in HIV-1 prevention strategies
NK cell responses can be autologous and/or alloreactive.

1) NK cells are important for HIV control, 2) NK cell activation is dependent on the balance of activating and inhibitory receptor/ligand bonds, 3) the presence of KIR/HLAMismatch is associated with resistance to both HIV-1 infection and disease progression, and 4) NK cell responses against donor-derived allogenic HIV infected cells can eliminate HIV before it can infect autologous cells
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role of NK cells and their receptors in HIV-1 infection and disease progression.
the role of KIR/HLAs in HIV-1 infection and disease progression, and the potential of alloreactive NK cells as a new strategy to control HIV-1 infection in the future.
the role of NK cells as a potential barrier to HIV transmission, and the role of NK cell activation in controlling HIV infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the role of NK cells, as well as their receptors and ligands, in HIV-1 outcome is complex and multifactorial, and that the influence of these factors on HIV-1 acquisition and progression is dependent on the specific setting.
the NK cell responses are important for both the acquisition and the progression of HIV-1, and that both autologous and allogeneic NK cell responses are involved.
NK cell-mediated resistance against HIV-1 is multifactorial.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the NK cell-mediated resistance to HIV-2 infection is more complex and multifactorial than previously thought.

NK cells play a role in protection against HIV-1, but that their effect is dependent on their activating and inhibitory receptor-ligate interactions with target cells, and on the route of transmission.
NK cell activation is associated with resistance to infection, but not necessarily with resistance to disease progression.
The main takeaway from our work is that
NK cells are an important component of the immune system in the fight against HIV-1.

the NK cell response in HIV-1 is complex, and that the interplay between activating and inhibitory KIR and HlA molecules, and the presence of iKIR/HA mismatches between donor and recipient, are likely to play a role in HIV-1 outcome.
both autologous as well as allogeneic NK cell responses are important in controlling HIV-1 infection and disease progression.
